name: Murata-grm_GRM21BR61H106KE43
title: 10 µF 50 V X5R multilayer ceramic chip capacitor, 0805

source.revision: Reference sheet GRM21BR61H106KE43-01A, specifications as of Jun.10,2026

summary: GRM21BR61H106KE43 is a 10 µF ±10 % multilayer ceramic capacitor rated 50 V DC, with X5R dielectric and a 2.0 × 1.25 × 1.25 mm (0805) body. It works from -55 to 85 °C and is limited to consumer equipment. It can be reflow or flow soldered, and comes on 180 mm or 330 mm reels of 8 mm plastic tape.

pins.function: Termination at one end of the chip; no polarity.
Termination at the other end; interchangeable with pin 1.

operation.text: X5R ceramic loses or gains up to 15 % of its capacitance across -55 to 85 °C. Where a circuit depends on a tight value, such as a timing network, the drift over the working temperature range has to be allowed for.

Capacitance is specified at 1 kHz and 1 Vrms. At high capacitance a meter's output voltage can drop, so the voltage actually across the part should be confirmed. The reading of a high dielectric constant part also shifts with the AC level applied.

Nothing across the terminals may exceed DC 50 V: with DC plus ripple the zero-to-peak value counts, with pure AC or pulses the peak-to-peak value, and surges and ESD are held to the same limit. Overvoltage breaks down the dielectric layers and leaves a short; how long that takes depends on the voltage and the ambient temperature.

AC or pulse current through the part warms it through dielectric loss. For parts rated below 100 VDC, the body should rise no more than 20 °C above a 25 °C ambient, and the surface temperature including that rise has to stay inside the 85 °C maximum.
A high dielectric constant ceramic loses capacitance as DC bias rises, and the rate of loss increases with voltage even below the rating.
High dielectric constant ceramics such as X5R lose capacitance slowly with time; C0G shows no change over the same period.

Bending or twisting of the board can crack the chip. Orient the chip to take the least strain from bending, keep it away from break-off lines and screw holes, add slits near separation lines, avoid pick-and-place nozzles pressing too low, support the board under test probes, and separate panels with a router where possible. A cracked part can lose insulation and short.
Parts removed from equipment are not to be reused. Long-stored parts should have their solderability checked and be heat-treated before capacitance is measured. Sn-Zn solder degrades reliability.

Both the board and the part are preheated so the step between solder and part surface stays within the allowed ΔT: 190 °C for reflow of the 21 size and 150 °C for flow. Reflow peaks at 240 to 260 °C; flow peaks at 250 to 260 °C for no more than 5 s. A peak below the solder supplier's recommended peak risks poor wetting, voids, whiskers, weak joints and tombstoning. Repeated passes count against the same time budget. Too much solder raises the fillet and the risk of cracking; too little lets the chip come away. In flow soldering the fillet should stay below the chip's own height.
Soldering time and temperature should keep termination leaching under 25 % of the end-face edge on a loose chip and under 25 % of the edge length once mounted.

Strain at the centre of a board bent between two supports grows with the span and shrinks as the board's width, elastic modulus and thickness increase; thickness enters squared, so it has the strongest effect.

Flux for flow soldering should be applied thinly and contain at most 0.1 % halide; strongly acidic flux or coating material corrodes the part. Ultrasonic cleaning can resonate the board and crack chips. Coating resins should shrink little on curing, match the chip's expansion and absorb little moisture; a silicone undercoat can cushion the stress, and epoxy is a low-moisture choice.

When the chip is glued down before flow soldering, the adhesive (typically epoxy) must hold through placement and soldering, resist moisture, keep its shape, cure quickly, insulate well, and be free of halogens and corrosives. Too little glue lets the chip drop off; too much spreads onto the lands; overcuring oxidises the terminations.

In service the part must be kept away from water, oil, condensation, direct sunlight, ozone, UV, radiation, corrosive gases and shock or vibration beyond its limits. Water or brine across the terminals shorts the part, and corrosive vapours degrade insulation. Under AC or pulse drive a high-permittivity chip vibrates piezoelectrically and can be audible.
A cracked chip can fail short. Where a short could cause shock, smoke or fire, the circuit needs a fail-safe such as a fuse. The series carries no safety-standard certification.

Life is quoted as the time to a 1 % cumulative failure rate in continuous use. General-application parts aim at about 10 years and consumer-specific parts, like this one, at over 5 years; either stretches longer when run at 80 % of rated voltage or less and at least 20 °C under the maximum operating temperature.

This part is limited to consumer equipment. The series is not intended for aircraft, aerospace, undersea, power plant control, medical, transportation, traffic control, disaster prevention, industrial data-processing or combustion control equipment, or anything of similar reliability demand.
